crime.value: Kidnapping-for-ransom of a shady rich man, $200,000 taken, kidnapper unidentified except for one telephoto payoff photo; central question: who is he and where is the money? Compounded by Blake's own attempted theft and killing of the kidnapper.
crime.quote: The only thing the police had on him was the telephoto shot taken at the moment of payoff.

victim.value: Johnny Roth, wealthy fringe-of-the-law figure caught in a congressional investigation, so he couldn't cooperate with police — making him safely kidnappable; later O'Steen himself, strangled by Blake.
victim.quote: When Johnny Roth got into that congressional investigation bind so he couldn't kick too much, I went after him.

closed_world.value: The city — stadium crowd, then O'Steen's fifth-floor apartment (number seven) in a quiet residential block, staked out by police; the final confrontation is sealed in that room.
closed_world.quote: The man stopped the car before a medium-sized apartment house.

culprit_and_motive.value: Ronald O'Steen, ex-college halfback too light for the pros, planned the kidnapping five years as his one 'big one'; Blake kills him for the same greed — 'because you're me.'
culprit_and_motive.quote: “So you went for the big one.” “Yes. I went for the big one.”

resolution.value: FBI traced the photo by checking old athlete newspaper pictures and staked out the apartment; Blake's recognition leads them to the money. O'Steen dies; Blake is ironically hailed a hero, his guilt unpunished except for suspicion.
resolution.quote: They decided he looked like an athlete, so they started checking newspaper pictures for boxers and football players

investigator.value: Blake, an aging veteran detective with a photographic memory for faces, near mandatory retirement — investigator who becomes the criminal.
investigator.quote: “I've got a talent,” he said. “I never forget a face.”

suspect_architecture.value: Effectively no suspect pool — an inverted crime story with two figures: Ronald O'Steen, the known kidnapper identified from the outset, and Blake, the detective who becomes the second criminal. Differentiation is by mirroring rather than by competing means/motive/opportunity: both are failed footballers, loners, waiting for 'the big one.'
suspect_architecture.quote: He was a loner, as Blake was a loner. Loner pitted against loner.

red_herring.value: Blake's own conduct functions as a herring in reverse: his shakedown of O'Steen is read by the captain as a brilliant undercover ruse to make the suspect reveal the money's location, misdirecting the institution away from his real corruption. The FBI agent's suspicion is the counterweight left unresolved.
red_herring.quote: "You made him think you were just after the money. You let him think it was a heist instead of an arrest."

clue_fairness.value: Fully fair — the reader is given every fact as Blake gets it: the trick memory for faces, the single telephoto payoff snapshot, the exit ramp FF, the airline satchel matching the photograph, and O'Steen's college football past. The stake-out reveal is retro-justified by the FBI's disclosed method (checking athletes' newspaper photos).
clue_fairness.quote: "They decided he looked like an athlete, so they started checking newspaper pictures for boxers and football players"

social_world.value: Institutional police hierarchy and its ceilings: a promotion ladder Blake has topped out on for lack of education, mandatory retirement in three months, precinct captain's patronage and 'implicit faith,' inter-agency friction between local police and a young dapper FBI agent, plus a kidnap victim (Johnny Roth) too compromised by a congressional investigation to call the law.
social_world.quote: "For years now he had been a full detective, having gone as far as a man with his education and attainments could hope to go."

alibi.value: No formal alibi contest. Blake's cover is his absence from duty — the captain assumes he 'had a live one' when he fails to call in — and his final alibi for the killing is the self-defence claim ('I can always claim I was making an arrest'), which the captain hands him unprompted.
alibi.quote: "Blake did not call in the next morning, though he was on duty for the day."

reveal_mechanic.value: Reversal by surveillance: the stake-out already in place means Blake's crime was observed all along, but the captain's faith re-narrates the evidence as heroism. The demonstration is the satchel — the same airline bag from the payoff photograph — opened in front of the money, and the trailed trip to the bank vault.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "We tailed you to the bank this morning," the FBI agent said.

media_and_audience.value: The crime is packaged for public consumption: television broadcast of the championship game triggers the recognition, a nationwide six-week manhunt runs on one blurred telephoto image, and the ending promises reporters, photographers and hero headlines — clippings Blake will reread in a retirement poisoned by what they omit.
media_and_audience.quote: "There'll be newspaper guys at the precinct, photographers, the whole works. Why, it's your greatest case, Blake."

investigator_wound.value: Blake's lifelong hunger for 'the big one' — the football glory denied him by poverty, then the career ceiling and imminent mandatory retirement — leaves him envious of the criminal he mirrors; the case exploits exactly that, turning his one gift (face memory) into the instrument of his corruption and murder.
investigator_wound.quote: All of his life he had been looking for the big one. First, he had thought to find it in football.

victims_enemies.value: The kidnap victim, Johnny Roth, was a shady rich man operating on the fringe of the law, caught in a congressional investigation — vulnerable precisely because he couldn't go to the police. O'Steen watched him five years and chose him for that vulnerability.
victims_enemies.quote: When Johnny Roth got into that congressional investigation bind so he couldn't kick too much, I went after him.

suspect_wounds.value: Blake's wound is the unfulfilled ambition — the football career he never had, the promotion ceiling he hit, mandatory retirement three months away. The recovered ransom activates a lifelong hunger for 'the big one' that thirty clean years had merely submerged.
suspect_wounds.quote: All of his life he had been looking for the big one. First, he had thought to find it in football.

unreliable_frame.value: The narrative is filtered through Blake's self-justifying consciousness; more sharply, the captain's reading of events is catastrophically wrong — he narrates Blake's attempted theft and murder as brilliant undercover police work, and Blake lets the false account stand.
unreliable_frame.quote: "You played it smart," he said. "You made him think you were just after the money."

setting_as_constraint.value: The televised championship game imposes a literal clock: Blake can only reach the stadium if the game goes into sudden-death overtime. Later the quiet apartment house, self-service elevator and empty carpeted hall permit a private arrest with no witnesses — but the thin walls let the stakeout hear the fight.
setting_as_constraint.quote: There would have to be a tie and a sudden death play-off to give him a chance at all.

evidence_type.value: Testimonial/visual recognition — a single blurred telephoto photograph of the payoff matched against a face glimpsed in a televised crowd shot, plus the FBI's documentary trawl of old newspaper sports photographs.
evidence_type.quote: They got a snap of you on the payoff. I was watching television yesterday and I saw you in the crowd.

false_suspect.value: Inverted: the guilty man, Blake, is universally taken as the hero. The dead O'Steen is credited with attacking him. Only the FBI agent's cold, unprovable suspicion survives.
false_suspect.quote: He looked at the FBI agent, recognized the residual suspicion. But there was no danger there.

technical_detail.value: Police craft: Blake's trained eidetic memory for faces, honed by years in the mug room — and the corollary that a first-time freelance criminal has never been mugged or fingerprinted, so only a photograph can identify him. The FBI's counterpart method: profiling the man as an athlete and searching old sports photos.
technical_detail.quote: He was the hardest of all to catch, a freelance criminal who had never fallen, never served time, never been mugged

moral_ambiguity.value: Blake is a thirty-year honest cop who never took a bribe, denied college and the pros by poverty, capped by education and facing forced retirement; he sees in O'Steen his own mirror — 'because you're me' — and his crime is the eruption of a lifetime of deferred, sublimated ambition rather than greed or cruelty.
moral_ambiguity.quote: Because you're me, and I'm you. But now I know I've got to kill you. For that same reason.

_meta.title: A Try for the Big Prize
_meta.author: BORDEN DEAL
